subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Non Exam Assessment Spoken Language Endorsement
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does it mean to say language 'changes over time'?
options: Spelling can never change
Words, meanings and usage shift across generations, with new words added and others fading
Only accents change, never words
People stop speaking entirely
questions.explain: Language evolves as new words appear, meanings shift and some terms become archaic.

questions.q: Which statement about regional dialect words is true?
options: They reflect local variation and identity, like 'bairn' for child in the North East
They are the same as RP
They are always incorrect English
They can only be written, never spoken
questions.explain: Dialect words show regional variation and identity and are a legitimate part of language.

questions.q: Which is the best example of 'colloquial' language?
options: I am writing to inform you of the situation.
Cheers, mate, that's well good.
I should be most grateful for your assistance.
The committee will reconvene at noon.
questions.explain: Colloquial language is informal, everyday speech, often using slang like 'mate' and 'well good'.

questions.q: Why might a speaker change their language depending on their audience?
options: Because language never changes
To make speech harder to follow
To confuse the listener
To suit the level of formality and ensure they are understood
questions.explain: Speakers adapt register and vocabulary to match context and audience for clarity and appropriateness.

questions.q: When giving a spoken presentation, why are pauses useful?
options: They confuse the audience deliberately
They show the speaker has forgotten everything
They allow ideas to land and give emphasis to key points
They make the presentation sound robotic
questions.explain: Well-placed pauses give the audience time to absorb ideas and add emphasis.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of spontaneous spoken language?
options: Numbered footnotes
Overlapping turns and interruptions between speakers
A formal contents page
Carefully edited final drafts
questions.explain: Real-time conversation often features overlaps and interruptions as speakers take turns.

questions.q: Which is an example of a filler used in spontaneous speech?
options: A full stop
A capital letter
'Erm' or 'you know'
A subheading
questions.explain: Fillers like 'erm' and 'you know' fill pauses while a speaker thinks in real time.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of spontaneous spoken language but not planned writing?
options: Fillers and false starts like 'um, I mean, the thing is...'
A clear title and headings
Footnotes
Carefully organised paragraphs
questions.explain: Spontaneous speech often contains fillers, false starts and self-correction.

questions.q: Which statement about accents is most accurate?
options: Accents only exist in informal speech
Everyone speaks with an accent of some kind
Only people from certain regions have an accent
An accent is a sign of poor education
questions.explain: Every speaker has an accent; it simply reflects how their pronunciation has developed.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of 'jargon'?
options: A filler such as 'um'
A regional word like 'barm' for bread roll
Words like 'gonna' and 'wanna'
Specialist terms such as a doctor saying 'myocardial infarction'
questions.explain: Jargon is specialist or technical vocabulary used within a particular profession or field.

questions.q: What is 'slang'?
options: Informal words and phrases often used by particular groups, e.g. 'lit', 'peng'
Punctuation marks
Technical medical terms
Formal vocabulary used in essays
questions.explain: Slang is very informal language, often group-specific and changing quickly.

questions.q: What is an 'idiolect'?
options: The unique language style of an individual person
A regional dialect
A type of formal jargon
The language of a whole country
questions.explain: An idiolect is the personal, individual way one person uses language.

questions.q: Which is a feature of an effective spoken presentation?
options: Clear pacing, eye contact and varied tone to engage the audience
Reading every word in a flat monotone
Mumbling and avoiding the audience
Speaking as fast as possible
questions.explain: Good presentations use pacing, eye contact and vocal variety to hold attention.

questions.q: Which statement about non-standard dialect grammar, such as 'I done it', is most accurate?
options: It should be corrected in every situation
It is a legitimate, rule-governed feature of a dialect, though not Standard English
It is a sign the speaker cannot think clearly
It is identical to Standard English
questions.explain: Non-standard dialect forms follow their own consistent rules and are valid varieties, distinct from Standard English.

questions.q: In a job interview, which language choice is most appropriate?
options: Heavy slang and casual fillers
Standard English with a polite, formal register
Whispering and mumbling
Specialist jargon the interviewer won't know
questions.explain: Formal contexts like interviews call for Standard English and a polite register.

questions.q: What is 'Standard English'?
options: Only the language used in poems
The slowest way of speaking
Any regional dialect
The variety of English widely accepted as correct in formal contexts
questions.explain: Standard English is the form recognised as correct for formal and official communication.

questions.q: Why do many people use more Standard English in formal situations than at home?
options: Because Standard English is always quicker to speak
Because non-standard forms are impossible to understand
Because Standard English carries prestige and is expected in formal contexts
Because regional dialects are banned
questions.explain: Standard English holds social prestige and is the expected form in formal or official settings.

questions.q: Which sentence uses 'non-standard' rather than Standard English?
options: We wasn't there yesterday.
We had not been there yesterday.
We were not there yesterday.
We weren't there yesterday.
questions.explain: 'We wasn't' is non-standard; Standard English requires 'we weren't'.

questions.q: Which best describes 'code-switching'?
options: Refusing to change how you speak in any situation
Switching between varieties of language depending on the context or audience
Writing in two languages at once
A type of punctuation error
questions.explain: Code-switching is moving between language varieties, such as dialect and Standard English, to suit the situation.

questions.q: What is the difference between formal and informal register?
options: Formal register is louder; informal register is quieter
Informal register can only be written, never spoken
Formal register suits official contexts and uses Standard English; informal register is relaxed and everyday
There is no real difference between them
questions.explain: Register varies with context: formal for official situations, informal for casual ones.

questions.q: What is 'Received Pronunciation' (RP)?
options: A written punctuation rule
A prestige accent traditionally associated with Standard English and the BBC
A type of slang
A regional accent from Yorkshire
questions.explain: RP is a prestige, non-regional accent historically linked to Standard English and broadcasting.

questions.q: How has technology most clearly affected language change in recent years?
options: It has made everyone speak Received Pronunciation
It has removed the need for Standard English
It has stopped all new words from forming
It has introduced new words and abbreviations such as 'selfie' and 'lol'
questions.explain: Digital communication has generated new vocabulary and abbreviations, showing language change in action.
